1G OurBigBook.com
Expand the finite Euler product into geometric series. By unique prime factorization, it is the sum of 1/n over positive integers whose prime factors do not exceed x, and hence contains every term up to m=⌊x⌋. The harmonic sum satisfies
∏p≤x​(1−p−1)−1≥∑n=1m​n1​>∫1m+1​tdt​=log(m+1)>logx.
(1)
The last inequality uses m+1>x, including when x is an integer. For each prime number p,
0<−log(1−p−1)−p−1=∑j=2∞​jpj1​<2p(p−1)1​.
(2)
The telescoping series over all integers n≥2 bounds the sum of these remainders by 21​∑n≥2​[n(n−1)]−1=1/2. Taking logarithms of the product bound therefore gives
p≤x∑​p1​>loglogx−21​,c=−21​.​
(3)
This explicit constant suffices; no asymptotic theorem about the distribution of prime numbers is needed.

For x>0, N(x)=⌊1/x⌋ and T(x)=1/x−⌊1/x⌋. Iterating this Gauss continued-fraction map on an irrational number never reaches zero, and its continued fraction is
x=[0;N(x),N(Tx),N(T2x),…].​
(4)
The branches T:(1/(n+1),1/n)→(0,1) have inverse xn​(y)=1/(n+y), for n≥1. The change of variables formula for a probability density function gives, almost everywhere,
fT(X)​(y)=∑n=1∞​f(n+y1​)(n+y)21​=log21​∑n=1∞​[n+y1​−n+y+11​]=(log2)(1+y)1​.
(5)
The endpoints of these branches are a countable set of probability zero. Thus T(X) and X have the same distribution; this Gauss measure is an invariant measure for the Gauss continued-fraction map.

3G (Coding & Cryptography)

Words: 234 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 234
3G OurBigBook.com
In the RSA cryptosystem, choose distinct large prime numbers p,q, set N=pq, and choose e coprime to φ(N)=(p−1)(q−1). Choose d with ed≡1(modφ(N)). A plaintext residue class m is encrypted as c=me(modN) and decrypted as cd(modN). Fermat's little theorem modulo p and q, followed by the Chinese remainder theorem, proves correctness even when m is not coprime to N.
Textbook RSA cryptosystem is multiplicative: E(m1​m2​)=E(m1​)E(m2​)(modN). For a chosen-ciphertext attack, multiply an intercepted c by re for a known invertible r. A decryption oracle returns mr, from which multiplication by r−1 recovers m. Likewise, multiplying two textbook RSA signatures produces a signature of their product. These are homomorphism attacks, exploiting algebra rather than factoring N.
For an ElGamal signature, choose a prime p, a primitive root g modulo p, a private exponent a, and public y=ga. To sign a message digest h=H(m), choose a fresh secret k coprime to p−1 and set
r=gk(modp),s=k−1(h−ar)(modp−1).​
(6)
Verification checks 1≤r≤p−1 and gH(m)≡yrrs(modp), which follows because ar+ks≡h(modp−1). Authenticating the ciphertext and its context with such a digital signature, before decryption, prevents the simple multiplicative modification from being accepted without a fresh valid signature. One needs an appropriate cryptographic hash function and fresh secret cryptographic nonces: this is not a claim that every algebraic attack is impossible. In particular, the unhashed historical ElGamal signature scheme admits existential forgeries of specially chosen message exponents; mere multiplication of encrypted messages is not an authentication mechanism.

a OurBigBook.com
Use state elimination for finite automata on a generalized finite automaton, whose directed edges are labelled by regular expressions. Add a fresh initial state s with an ε-edge to the old initial state and a fresh final state f with ε-edges from all old accepting states. Every missing edge has label ∅, the empty language; parallel edges are merged by union. The label ε denotes the language containing just the empty word.
When eliminating a state k, replace the label on each surviving edge i→j by
Rij​ ∪ Rik​(Rkk​)∗Rkj​.​
(7)
Here juxtaposition means concatenation of formal languages, and the Kleene star allows zero or more traversals of the loop at k. Then delete k and its incident edges. Eliminate every original state; the remaining s→f label is a regular expression for exactly the accepted formal language. The update accounts for paths avoiding k and paths entering k, looping there any number of times, and leaving it.

b

Words: 199 Articles: 1
4H OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 199
b OurBigBook.com
Let K be the diagonal halting set, which is undecidable. The pumping argument below actually holds for every subset K⊆N; nonregularity needs the stated convention, or at least a set of exponents whose unary language is nonregular.
The pumping lemma for regular languages holds with pumping length one. For an accepted nonempty word, pump its first symbol. A word containing only 1s remains in 1∗ even if that symbol is deleted. If there is a zero and a nonempty prefix before its last zero, pumping the first symbol leaves the last zero and its following n∈K ones unchanged. If the word is 01n, pumping its initial zero produces 0i1n; this is accepted for i≥1, and for i=0 it belongs to 1∗. In every case the pumped substring is nonempty and lies in the first position.
If L were a regular language, closure under intersection would make
L∩01∗={01n:n∈K}
(8)
regular. A finite-state automaton for this intersection would decide membership of n in the diagonal halting set by reading 01n, a contradiction. Thus L satisfies the pumping lemma but is not regular, under the usual meaning of K. If K were arbitrary, the printed conclusion would be false, for example for K=N.

a OurBigBook.com
This is the appropriate command for the full contingency table. It fits a log-linear model to the nine cell counts, with logarithmic link function and no interaction:
Yij​∼Poisson(μij​),logμij​=α+gi​+dj​.
(9)
With baseline constraints on gi​,dj​, there are five parameters. The factorized means express independence of treatment group and damage category. The maximum-likelihood estimates are
μ​ij​=Y++​Yi+​Y+j​​=(18,4,8)in each row.​
(10)
Although the experiment fixes each row total at 30, conditioning these independent Poisson random variables on those totals produces the appropriate row-wise multinomial distribution. The Poisson trick therefore gives the correct likelihood inference for this independence log-linear model for a two-way contingency table; the margins are nuisance parameters. It tests whether treatment changes the distribution of damage, rather than modelling a binary outcome.

b

Words: 83 Articles: 1
5J OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 83
b OurBigBook.com
This is not a valid ordinary R glm family specification. A multinomial distribution is natural for the three damage counts conditional on the row total, but base R's generalized linear model interface does not supply a family named multinomial. Furthermore, the written response is one cell count, not a three-category response or grouped multinomial vector. A properly specified multinomial logistic regression could model category probabilities by group, but it is not the model fit by this command. The independent-count log-linear model in part (a), conditional on the margins, is the appropriate supplied alternative.

c

Words: 79 Articles: 1
5J OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 79
c OurBigBook.com
This does not model the full three-category response. A binomial distribution has two outcome classes, whereas the observed damage factor has three. In base R, a factor response to a binomial generalized linear model is coded as first level versus all other levels; this would silently collapse the categories. It would also treat the nine table rows as nine individual observations, ignoring the frequencies. A deliberate binary analysis would require specifying the collapse and retaining the counts, but cannot recover the full damage distribution.

d

Words: 75 Articles: 1
5J OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 75
d OurBigBook.com
The count weights correct the loss of frequencies for a deliberately coarsened binary response, but do not supply a third outcome category. Thus this remains inappropriate for the full contingency table. With the base R factor convention, it could fit the chosen first damage level versus the other two combined, using a logistic regression and the frequencies as weights. That is a different scientific question. The supplied log-linear model retains all three categories and their counts without this information loss.

6B OurBigBook.com
At an endemic equilibrium, I∗​>0, so βS∗​=μ+ν. Substitution into the susceptible equation gives
S∗​=R0​N​,I∗​=μ+νμN​(1−R0​1​).​
(11)
These values are physically positive exactly when R0​>1. The Jacobian matrix at this equilibrium is
J=(−μR0​μ(R0​−1)​−(μ+ν)0​),trJ=−μR0​<0,detJ=μ(μ+ν)(R0​−1)>0.
(12)
Both eigenvalues have negative real parts, so the endemic equilibrium is locally asymptotically stable. Its decay exponents are
λ±​=−2μR0​​±4μ2R02​​−μ(μ+ν)(R0​−1)​.
(13)
The regime ν≫μ means recovery is rapid compared with demographic replacement. For fixed R0​>1 away from the threshold, the exponents form a complex conjugate pair with frequency approximately μν(R0​−1)​. Hence
T≃μν(R0​−1)​2π​.​
(14)
Strictly, oscillations require μ(μ+ν)(R0​−1)>μ2R02​/4; ν≫μ alone does not ensure this uniformly for every R0​ arbitrarily close to one or arbitrarily large.
Vaccinating a fraction v of newborns replaces the susceptible input by μN(1−v). The effective basic reproduction number is Rv​=(1−v)R0​, and the same calculation replaces R0​ by Rv​. Provided Rv​>1 and the oscillatory approximation remains applicable, vaccination lengthens the oscillation period, because Rv​−1 is smaller. Extremely near eradication the exponents become real and there is no oscillation period to extrapolate indefinitely.

7E OurBigBook.com
Substitute the Laplace contour-integral method for a linear differential equation into the differential equation and use zezt=∂t​ezt. Integration by parts around a closed contour avoiding singularities gives
0=∫C​ezt{−[(1+t2)f(t)]′−2tf(t)}dt.
(15)
It suffices to solve (1+t2)f′+4tf=0, giving
f(t)=(1+t2)2C0​​.​
(16)
Nonzero contour integrals arise by enclosing one or both double poles t=±i. At t=i, the residue is
Rest=i​(1+t2)2ezt​=−41​(z+i)eiz.
(17)
The conjugate pole gives the conjugate expression for real z. Taking real and imaginary linear combinations yields the real solutions
y1​(z)=sinz−zcosz,y2​(z)=cosz+zsinz.​
(18)
Their derivatives are y1′​=zsinz, y2′​=zcosz, and their Wronskian is −z2, so they are linearly independent on every interval avoiding zero. Both extend analytically across zero and remain independent as functions; the vanishing Wronskian at zero reflects the singular leading coefficient of the printed differential equation there.

The Poisson bracket is {f,g}=r⋅(∇f×∇g). Since ∇ρ2=2r, the scalar triple product vanishes, and
{f,ρ2}=0.​
(19)
Equivalently, check the identity on x,y,z and extend to every polynomial using the Leibniz rule. Thus ρ2 is a Casimir function of a Poisson manifold of this rotational Lie-Poisson structure on R3.
The Hamilton's equations are
x˙=(B−C)yz,y˙​=(C−A)xz,z˙=(A−B)xy.​
(20)
Linearization about (1,0,0) gives α˙=0, β˙​=(C−A)γ, γ˙​=(A−B)β. The two nonzero exponents satisfy λ2=(C−A)(A−B). Consequently
exponential instability occurs iff min(B,C)<A<max(B,C).​
(21)
When A is outside this interval the transverse motion is oscillatory. At equality the linearization is nonhyperbolic; if just one transverse coupling vanishes, the other permits secular linear growth, rather than an exponential instability. This is the familiar intermediate-axis instability described by the Euler equations for a torque-free rigid body.

a OurBigBook.com
For a thin spherical shell, the radial pressure force per unit volume is −dP/dr. By the shell theorem, the inward gravitational acceleration is GM(r)/r2, because exterior spherical shells contribute no force. Balancing force densities in hydrostatic equilibrium gives
drdP​=−r2GM(r)ρ(r)​,drdM​=4πr2ρ(r).​
(22)
The second equation is mass conservation; it closes the pressure-support equation once an equation of state is supplied.

Solution

b OurBigBook.com
Regularity at the centre requires finite ρc​,Pc​ and M(0)=0. Then M(r)=4πρc​r3/3+o(r3), so P′(0)=0. At a free stellar surface, P(R)=0; more generally it matches the external pressure. For P=Kρ2 with K>0 and vacuum outside, this also gives ρ(R)=0.
Inside the star, cancel positive ρ to obtain 2Kρ′=−GM/r2. Differentiate and use mass conservation:
r21​drd​(r2ρ′)=−K2πG​ρ.
(23)
Thus the Lane-Emden equation of polytropic index one is
x21​dxd​(x2dxdρ​)=−ρ,x=αr,α=K2πG​​.​
(24)
For example, the regular solution is ρ=ρc​sinx/x, with its central value interpreted by continuity, and the first vacuum surface is at x=π. This also verifies the stated central and surface boundary conditions.

a OurBigBook.com
Dirichlet theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions states that if positive integer q and integer a satisfy gcd(a,q)=1, then infinitely many prime numbers satisfy
p≡a(modq).​
(25)
The coprimality hypothesis is essential: if a and q have a common factor greater than one, a prime in the progression must divide that factor, giving at most finitely many possibilities.

Solution

Words: 133
b OurBigBook.com
Write an integral binary quadratic form as Q(u,v)=Au2+Buv+Cv2, with discriminant of a binary quadratic form d=B2−4AC. If Q(u,v)=p is prime, then gcd(u,v)=1: any common divisor would have its square dividing p. Complete (u,v) to a matrix in SL2​(Z) using Bezout identity. After the associated integral change of variables, the properly equivalent form has leading coefficient p, say [p,b,c]. Its discriminant of a binary quadratic form gives d=b2−4pc, hence b2≡d(modp).
Conversely suppose b02​≡d(modp). Since d is an integral-form discriminant of a binary quadratic form, d≡0 or 1(mod4). Choose b≡b0​(modp) with even integer parity for d≡0(mod4) and odd integer parity for d≡1(mod4). This is possible because p is odd. Then b2−d is divisible by 4p, and
Q(u,v)=pu2+buv+4pb2−d​v2​
(26)
is an integral form of discriminant of a binary quadratic form d representing p=Q(1,0). This proves the discriminant criterion for prime representation by a binary quadratic form, including the case p∣d; no assumption that d is a fundamental discriminant was used.

c

Words: 186 Articles: 1
10G OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 186
c OurBigBook.com
Both forms have discriminant of a binary quadratic form −60. The reduction algorithm for a positive definite binary quadratic form gives ∣b∣≤a≤c and a≤60/3​<5 for a reduced positive definite representative. Enumerating a=1,2,3,4 gives
[1,0,15],[2,2,8],[3,0,5],[4,2,4].
(27)
The second and fourth forms are imprimitive and represent only even integers. Every odd prime represented by a form of discriminant of a binary quadratic form −60 must therefore be represented by f or g.
For a prime p∤30, quadratic reciprocity gives
(p−60​)=(p−3​)(p5​)=(3p​)(5p​).
(28)
Every prime p≡1(mod15) has this symbol equal to one and hence is represented by one of the two primitive forms, by part (b). But an odd prime represented by g and different from three is 2(mod3), so these primes must be represented by f. Similarly, primes p≡2(mod15) have both symbols equal to −1, and are represented by g, since a prime represented by f is 1(mod3). Both residue classes are coprime to 15, so Dirichlet theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions proves each form represents infinitely many primes.
The same modulo-three distinction excludes every prime other than three from being represented by both. The form f does not represent three; g represents three and five but neither is represented by f, and two is represented by neither. Therefore there are no primes represented by both forms.

Let u(t)=γ(t)/∣γ(t)∣, a continuous map into the unit circle. By uniform continuity, partition [0,1] so finely that on each interval beginning at tj​, ∣u(t)/u(tj​)−1∣<1. This ratio lies in the right half-plane and has a continuous complex argument with value zero at tj​. Starting from θ0​, add these local arguments successively, matching endpoint values. This constructs a continuous real lift with u(t)=eiθ(t).
Any two such lifts with the same initial value differ by a continuous function taking values in 2πZ, and hence coincide. Since the curve closes, ei(θ(1)−θ(0))=1. Define its winding number by
w(γ)=2πθ(1)−θ(0)​∈Z.​
(29)
Changing the chosen initial argument adds a constant multiple of 2π to the whole lift, so the winding number is independent of that choice. No differentiability of the curve is required.

w(γm​)=m,m∈Z.​
(30)
Positive and negative integers correspond to opposite senses of traversal, and the constant curve gives zero.

Choose continuous argument lifts θ1​,θ2​ for the two curves. Their sum is a lift for their pointwise product, because
γ1​(t)γ2​(t)=∣γ1​(t)∣∣γ2​(t)∣ei(θ1​(t)+θ2​(t)).
(31)
Subtract its initial value from its final value to obtain
w(γ1​γ2​)=w(γ1​)+w(γ2​).​
(32)
In particular, winding numbers subtract under pointwise division of curves avoiding zero.

The continuous closed curve q(t)=γ2​(t)/γ1​(t) satisfies ∣q(t)−1∣<1. It lies in the right half-plane, which admits a single continuous complex argument in (−π/2,π/2). Since q closes, this argument has equal endpoint values, giving w(q)=0. Additivity under multiplication then yields
w(γ2​)=w(γ1​)+w(q)=w(γ1​).​
(33)
The strict inequality ensures that the quotient stays in a region avoiding zero and admitting a single argument branch.

e OurBigBook.com
The appropriate homotopy invariance of winding number is: if H:[0,1]2→C∖{0} is continuous and H(s,0)=H(s,1) for each s, then all loops t↦H(s,t) have the same winding number. The basepoint may move; every intermediate curve must close and avoid zero.
Compactness gives m=mins,t​∣H(s,t)∣>0. Uniform continuity gives δ>0 such that ∣s−s′∣<δ implies ∣H(s,t)−H(s′,t)∣<m for every t. Part (d) then makes the winding numbers equal for nearby s,s′. Subdivide [0,1] into steps smaller than δ and chain these equalities. Therefore
w(H(0,⋅))=w(H(1,⋅)).​
(34)
This proves the theorem directly for continuous loops, without requiring an integral formula or smooth homotopy.

Use fit.3 if backward selection is intended to combine adjacent periods. Each cumulative indicator is a separate model term; deleting its coefficient enforces equality of the two adjacent period means separated by that boundary. This offers an interpretable reduced stepwise profile. Fit.2 treats the entire factor as one term, so ordinary term-wise backward selection retains all five contrasts or removes period altogether. Removing selected baseline contrasts by hand would instead privilege period one, rather than grouping neighbouring periods. If the scientific objective were simply whether any period effect exists, retaining or deleting the whole factor in fit.2 would be the appropriate different procedure.

Solution

Under fit.2, observations in each period are independent Poisson random variables with a common mean, so each sample variance should fluctuate around its sample mean. The plot instead has variances roughly 130–300 for means roughly 80–120, well above the line variance equals mean. This is overdispersion.
Day-to-day traffic variation can produce a Poisson mixture: a random daily intensity increases the marginal variance and can correlate observations from the same day. A useful replacement is a negative binomial regression, with variance μ+μ2/κ, or a Poisson generalized linear mixed model with a day random intercept. A day-factor effect can also be included if inference is restricted to the observed days. A Quasi-Poisson regression estimates a dispersion multiplier for uncertainty, but does not itself explain the shared-day dependence and has no ordinary likelihood-based AIC. The means can retain the period-factor or selected jump structure.

Use the convention that the transitive closure of x is the least transitive set containing x as a subset. Define x0​=x and xn+1​=⋃xn​. For each natural number n, a finite sequence of length n+1 with these properties exists by induction, and is unique because each next entry is the uniquely determined union of the previous entry. Thus the relation sending n to its last entry is a definable function-class, not just a putative recursive specification. The Axiom schema of replacement applied to ω gives the set of all xn​. The Axiom of union then gives
TC(x)=n<ω⋃​xn​.​
(47)
If a∈xn​ and b∈a, then b∈xn+1​, so this set is transitive. It contains x=x0​, and any transitive set containing x contains all xn​ by induction; hence it is least. The convention requiring x itself as an element instead uses TC({x}).
The Axiom of foundation says every nonempty set A has an element a∈A with a∩A=∅. Epsilon induction says that for every formula ϕ,
[∀x((∀y∈xϕ(y))⇒ϕ(x))]⇒∀xϕ(x).
(48)
To derive induction from Foundation, if ϕ(x) fails, form by axiom schema of separation the nonempty set of counterexamples in TC({x}). A Foundation-minimal counterexample has every member satisfying ϕ, by transitivity, contradicting the inductive hypothesis. Conversely, if a nonempty set A has no Foundation-minimal member, every x∈A has a member in A. The formula x∈/A is then progressive: if all members of x are outside A, x must also be outside A. Epsilon induction makes A empty, a contradiction. Thus the two principles are equivalent given the other axioms.
The epsilon-recursion theorem states that for a definable class operation G assigning a unique set to each set-indexed function, there is a unique definable function-class F such that F(x)=G(F∣x​) for every set x. A version with explicit x in the argument is equivalent. Foundation gives well-foundedness and Replacement makes each restriction set-sized. Its ordinal restriction gives transfinite recursion and constructs the printed Cα​.
Here “countable” means at most countable, including finite sets and the empty set. By transfinite induction each Cα​ is transitive, each of its elements is countable, and Cα​⊆Cα+1​. At a successor this follows because a member of Cα​ is a countable subset of Cα​; at a limit use the increasing union. Let ω1​ be the first uncountable ordinal. Every countable subset of Cω1​​ lies in some Cα​ with α<ω1​, since countably many countable ordinal bounds have a countable supremum. It therefore belongs to Cα+1​. Consequently
Cω1​+1​=Cω1​​.​
(49)
There is no earlier stabilization: for every countable ordinal α, induction gives α⊆Cα​, so α∈Cα+1​, while Cα​⊆Vα​ excludes α by its rank. Thus ω1​ is the first such stage. The fixed set is the set of hereditarily countable sets.

A cyclotomic field over Q is a field Q(ζm​) generated by an mth root of unity of exact order m. It contains all roots of Xm−1, and is its splitting field. In characteristic zero this polynomial is separable, so the extension is Galois.
Every automorphism sends ζm​ to ζma​ with a∈(Z/mZ)×, and is determined by that image. Composition multiplies the exponents modulo m, yielding an injective homomorphism into an abelian group. Thus the Galois group is abelian. Using irreducibility of the cyclotomic polynomial, every unit exponent occurs and
Gal(Q(ζm​)/Q)≅(Z/mZ)×.​

If “cyclotomic” is used more broadly for a subfield of such a field, it is still Galois and abelian, because every subgroup of an abelian Galois group is normal.

Triangulate the sphere by the boundary complex of the cross-polytope with simplicial vertices ±e0​,…,±en​: a face contains at most one simplicial vertex from each antipodal pair. Take its barycentric subdivision. Its simplicial vertices are the nonempty faces F of the original complex, and its simplices are strictly nested chains F0​⊂⋯⊂Fk​.
Form a quotient complex whose simplicial vertices are pairs {F,−F}, and whose simplices are the images of these chains. No chain contains both F and −F. Moreover a chain of face-orbits lifts uniquely up to simultaneous negation: after choosing a largest face, every smaller face has at most one representative contained in it, because an original face contains no antipodal simplicial vertices. Thus the quotient is an honest simplicial complex, without two different simplices with the same simplicial vertex set. Its realization is homeomorphic to the sphere modulo its antipodal action. This provides a triangulation of Real projective space RPn. The subdivision avoids the duplicate-simplex problem of naively identifying simplicial vertices in the unsubdivided cross-polytope boundary.

For a nonsingular projective integral curve, apply the Riemann-Roch theorem to the divisor on an algebraic curve mP. It gives ℓ(mP)≥mdegP+1−g, where g is the geometric genus. For sufficiently large m, this exceeds the dimension of the space of constant functions; over the usual geometrically integral convention that dimension is one. An M/M/1 queue has a Poisson arrival process of rate λ, independent exponential service times of rate μ, and one server, with an unlimited waiting room and the usual first-come-first-served discipline. Its number-in-system process is a continuous-time birth-death chain with qj,j+1​=λ and qj,j−1​=μ for j≥1. For ρ=λ/μ<1, detailed balance gives
πj​=(1−ρ)ρj,j=0,1,….​
(99)
This sums to one and satisfies πj​λ=πj+1​μ. The nonexplosive irreducible chain therefore has an invariant probability and is positive recurrent. Equivalently its negative drift above zero gives finite mean return cycles. Here queue length includes the customer in service.
In equilibrium, PASTA gives an arriving customer's number of predecessors the distribution π. Conditional on j predecessors, memoryless property makes its total waiting-plus-service time a sum of j+1 independent Exp(μ) variables. Its Laplace transform is
∑j=0∞​(1−ρ)ρj(μ+sμ​)j+1=μ−λ+sμ−λ​.
(100)
Therefore
W∼Exp(μ−λ).​
(101)
This is the sojourn time including service, not just the time until service begins.

∑j=1∞​δ(1−δ)j−1(μ+sμ​)j=δμ+sδμ​.

Btotal​∼Exp(δμ).​

This excludes the waiting between visits. A feedback completion changes the customer's position but not the number in the system. By exponential memoryless property, the latter process has births of rate λ and true deaths of rate δμ while nonempty; unsuccessful completions are self-events. It is therefore an M/M/1 number process with effective service rate δμ, giving
λ<δμ,πj​=(1−δμλ​)(δμλ​)j.​

For positive λ equality is null recurrent, larger arrival rate is unstable, and δ=0 admits no departure-based equilibrium.
To prove the output claim, state the relevant time reversal of a continuous-time Markov chain theorem: an equilibrium continuous-time chain satisfying detailed balance has the same reversed path law. In this reversible birth-death process, final departures are precisely downward jumps; time reversal turns them into upward jumps. Upward jumps are supplied by a state-independent Poisson clock of rate λ, so their process is Poisson. Hence the stationary final-departure process is Poisson of rate λ. This is the output conclusion of Burke theorem for the effective number process; it does not say the process of all service completions has that rate.

Assume a finite optimum with X>0 and continuous price near its completion time. With costate p∗ for the remaining-file state, the minimization Hamiltonian of an optimal-control problem is H=u(p(t)−p∗). It is independent of x, so p∗ is constant. By the Pontryagin maximum principle, pointwise minimization over [0,1] gives
u(t)=1 if p(t)<p∗,u(t)=0 if p(t)>p∗.​
(117)
This is a bang-bang control away from equality. At equality partial transmission or either endpoint rate is allowed. This also follows by exchanging a small amount of transmission from a more expensive time to a cheaper unused time. The free-terminal-time transversality condition is minu​H(T,u)+2γT=0. Since T>0, it forces p∗>p(T) and terminal transmission at rate one, yielding
p∗=p(T)+2γT.​
(118)
Without regularity/existence hypotheses an arbitrary known price need not have a finite differentiable optimum; the equality is the interior terminal-time condition used here.
For p(t)=t+1/t, X=1, feasible completion requires T>1 for finite cost. The price decreases to its minimum at one and then increases. Its cheapest unrestricted interval of length one has endpoints a,a+1 of equal price, giving a(a+1)=1 and a+1=φ=(1+5​)/2. For 1<T≤φ, the cheapest length-one subset of [0,T] is the terminal interval [T−1,T]: its left endpoint has at least the price of its right endpoint, and the earlier times are still more expensive. For T≥φ the transmission minimum is unchanged from that unrestricted interval, while the delay cost increases, so no optimum lies beyond φ.
For the terminal-interval policy the total cost is
J(T)=T−21​+logT−1T​+γT2,J′(T)=1−T(T−1)1​+2γT.
(119)
Its derivative is strictly increasing on T>1, since J′′(T)=(2T−1)/[T2(T−1)2]+2γ>0. It is negative near one and positive at φ, so the unique global optimum is
u=1 on [T−1,T],u=0 earlier,(T−1)T1​=1+2γT.​
(120)
There is exactly one positive root: none lies in (0,1) because the left side is negative, and the strictly monotone comparison gives exactly one in (1,φ). Its threshold is p(T−1)=p(T)+2γT.

each Fourier component satisfies un=cos(nη)u0+k[sin(nη)/sinη]v0, where cosη=1−2μsin2(θ/2). Taking the limiting values at repeated roots and using ∣sin(nη)∣≤n∣sinη∣ gives ∣un∣≤∣u0∣+nk∣v0∣. This is a uniform finite-time stability bound in the physical displacement/velocity data and includes μ=1. A strict root-condition test for arbitrary two-level data must record the double-root qualification rather than calling that endpoint unconditionally power-bounded.
